title: Root-group products and pinned Weyl representatives over arbitrary rings
statement:
Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring and $(G,T=D_A(M),\Phi,\Phi^\vee,\Delta,(X_\alpha))$ a pinned split realization [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. Put $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ and let $\Phi^+$ be the roots positive relative to $\Delta$. For every $\gamma\in\Phi$, the additive group of the free rank-one module $\mathfrak g_\gamma$ has a canonical closed group homomorphism $\exp_\gamma$ into $G$, characterized by its differential being the inclusion and by $T$-equivariance. Its image $U_\gamma$ is a root subgroup, and
$$t\exp_\gamma(v)t^{-1}=\exp_\gamma(\gamma(t)v).$$
The notation for the additive group means $R\mapsto R\otimes_A\mathfrak g_\gamma$ on commutative $A$-algebras $R$. These maps commute with arbitrary base change. If a reductive closed subgroup $K\subseteq G$ contains $T$ and has a root $\gamma$ of $G$, its $\gamma$-root module and root exponential are the ones in $G$. Its coroot for $\gamma$ is also the original $\gamma^\vee$.

For $\alpha\in\Delta$ there is a unique linked generator $Y_{-\alpha}$ of $\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$ for which
$$n_\alpha=\exp_\alpha(X_\alpha)\exp_{-\alpha}(-Y_{-\alpha})\exp_\alpha(X_\alpha)$$
normalizes $T$. This element acts on $T$ by $s_\alpha(t)=t\alpha^\vee(\alpha(t))^{-1}$, conjugates $U_\gamma$ onto $U_{s_\alpha\gamma}$, and satisfies
$$n_\alpha^2=\alpha^\vee(-1),\qquad (n_\alpha\exp_\alpha(X_\alpha))^3=1.$$
The same construction in a reductive closed subgroup containing $T$ and $U_{\pm\alpha}$ gives the same linked generator and $n_\alpha$. The quotient sheaf $N_G(T)/T$ is the constant Weyl group generated by the $s_\alpha$. In particular, for distinct $\alpha,\beta\in\Delta$, if $m_{\alpha\beta}$ is the order of $s_\alpha s_\beta$ in that finite group, then $t_{\alpha\beta}:=(n_\alpha n_\beta)^{m_{\alpha\beta}}$ belongs to $T(A)$.

A subset $\Psi\subseteq\Phi$ is called closed here if it contains every root that is a nonempty sum of elements of $\Psi$. If $\Psi$ is closed and $\Psi\cap(-\Psi)=\varnothing$, multiplication in any enumeration identifies $\prod_{\gamma\in\Psi}U_\gamma$ with a smooth closed subgroup $U_\Psi$ of $G$, independent of the enumeration. In particular, for distinct simple roots $\alpha,\beta$, this applies to $\Psi_{\alpha\beta}=\Phi\cap\{i\alpha+j\beta:i,j\in\mathbf Z_{\geq0},\ i+j>0\}$; conjugation by $n_\alpha$ carries $U_c$ into $U_{\Psi_{\alpha\beta}}$ for $c\in\Psi_{\alpha\beta}\setminus\{\alpha\}$, and likewise for $\beta$.

Multiplication identifies $U_{-\Phi^+}\times_A T\times_A U_{\Phi^+}$ with an open subscheme $\Omega\subseteq G$, and $\Omega\times_A\Omega\to G$ by multiplication is faithfully flat and locally of finite presentation. Consequently $T$ and all the $U_\gamma$ generate $G$ as a sheaf for flat finitely presented coverings. One has $Z_G(T)=T$. The semisimple rank of every geometric fibre is $\dim_{\mathbf Q}\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf Q}(\Phi)$. All assertions permit disconnected and nonreduced $A$, and empty roots.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.4, printed pp.110,116--118; Corollary 5.1.9 and Remark 5.1.10, pp.140--142; Proposition 5.1.6 and Corollary 5.1.11, pp.138,142--143; Theorem 5.1.13 and Proposition 5.1.16, pp.143--148; Section 6.2 opening paragraph, p.198 (the fppf multiplication of two open cells). Coroots are constructed inside the rank-one centralizer in Section 4.2; self-centralizing tori are Proposition 3.1.9(2), pp.85--86; root rank is the classical root-datum rank of Section 1.3. Read online; local archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this reductive-group result.

proof.text: Choose generators of the finitely many free root lines, retaining the specified simple-root generators. Apply [lem-sfb-reductive-framed-noetherian-descent] to this full weight decomposition. It gives a Noetherian subring $A_0$, a reductive pair $(G_0,T_0)$ with exactly these free root lines, and its identification after base change with $(G,T)$. Apply [lem-sfb-relative-canonical-root-exponential] over $A_0$ and pull back its closed homomorphisms to $A$. Their domains identify with the additive root lines by the tangent comparison in the descent statement. They have the required differential, equivariance and geometric root-group fibres. This proves existence over $A$ without assuming $A$ Noetherian. The same construction is available to any reductive pair with a framed constant finite root set, without a pinning.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.4, pp.110,116--118; finite-presentation reduction used only to apply existing Noetherian DAG input.

proof.text: Fix a root $\gamma$. Let $H=Z_G(T_\gamma)$ be the rank-one centralizer of [lem-sfb-relative-root-rank-one-centralizer] and choose $\lambda\in M^\vee$ with $n=\langle\gamma,\lambda\rangle>0$. By [lem-sfb-relative-dynamic-subgroups], the attracting subgroup $V=U_H(\lambda)$ is smooth and connected on geometric fibres, with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g_\gamma$. On geometric fibres it is the $\gamma$-root group by [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations]. The exponential from step 1 lands in $H$ by $T_\gamma$-equivariance and in $V$ by contraction. Its map to $V$ is an isomorphism on geometric fibres: an equivariant map between the two copies of $\mathbf G_a$ has polynomial $f(z)=cz$, since $f(t^nz)=t^nf(z)$ and comparison of Laurent coefficients kills all degrees except one; its differential makes $c$ a unit. By [lem-sfb-flat-geometric-fibre-open-criterion], this map between smooth finitely presented schemes is an isomorphism over $A$. Every other equivariant homomorphism with the same differential also factors through $V$. In the resulting coordinate on $V$, the same Laurent-polynomial calculation over $A$ gives $f(z)=z$. This proves uniqueness, over nonreduced rings as well.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.4 proof, pp.116--118: factorization into the attracting root group and character, not differential-character, uniqueness.

proof.text: The existence and uniqueness argument also works over each nonzero $A$-algebra $R$: [lem-sfb-pinned-split-root-base-change] identifies its root line with $R\otimes_A\mathfrak g_\gamma$. The pullback of $\exp_\gamma$ has the prescribed differential and full torus equivariance there, so uniqueness identifies it with the exponential constructed over $R$. Successive base changes give the same map for the same reason. Over the zero algebra the assertion is the unique map between empty schemes. The equation $t\exp_\gamma(v)t^{-1}=\exp_\gamma(\gamma(t)v)$ is exactly the established equivariance, on all algebra points.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.4, base-change assertion and uniqueness proof.

proof.text: For $\alpha\in\Delta$ retain $H=Z_G(T_\alpha)$. Its weights are $0,\alpha,-\alpha$ and its two root lines are free. Applying [lem-sfb-reductive-framed-noetherian-descent] to $H$ gives a Noetherian rank-one model. Apply [lem-sfb-relative-rank-one-local-matrix-model] there and pull its affine-open cover back to $A$. Thus locally $(H,T)$ is a central split torus times $\operatorname{SL}_2$, $\operatorname{PGL}_2$ or $\operatorname{GL}_2$, with $\alpha$ the upper-root character. By step 2 the root maps in these models are precisely the upper/lower unipotent matrices with their derivative coordinates. Write $X_\alpha=xE_{12}$, $x\in A^\times$, locally, and set $Y_{-\alpha}=x^{-1}E_{21}$. The matrix product defining $n_\alpha$ is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&x\cr -x^{-1}&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. If instead $Y=yE_{21}$ is a generator and the product normalizes the diagonal torus, its lower-left entry $-y$ is a unit. It must therefore be in the antidiagonal normalizer component; its diagonal entries $1-xy$ vanish, so $y=x^{-1}$. This proves uniqueness even over disconnected rings, component by component. The affine-open cover is fpqc by [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-finer-than-etale]. The local choices agree and descend by [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent].

source.place: Corollary 5.1.9 proof, pp.140--142, using Theorem 5.1.8, pp.139--140.

proof.text: In the matrices of step 4, conjugation by $n_\alpha$ interchanges the two diagonal entries. For the ratio character this is $t\mapsto t\alpha^\vee(\alpha(t))^{-1}$, with coroot $c\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(c,c^{-1})$ in $\operatorname{SL}_2$ or $\operatorname{GL}_2$, and its image in $\operatorname{PGL}_2$. These coroots equal the prescribed ones: they agree on every geometric fibre, and [lem-sfb-relative-split-torus-matrix-sheaf] makes homomorphisms between split tori locally constant integer matrices, hence detected by geometric fibres. Direct multiplication gives $n_\alpha^2=\alpha^\vee(-1)$ and, putting $u=\exp_\alpha(X_\alpha)$, $n_\alpha u=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&x\cr -x^{-1}&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, whose square is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&-x\cr x^{-1}&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and whose cube is $1$. The computations descend to $G$ and remain valid in characteristics $2$ and $3$. Conjugation by $n_\alpha$ takes the $\gamma$-root line to the $s_\alpha\gamma$-line; composing its conjugate root map with this linear identification and applying uniqueness from step 2 proves $n_\alpha U_\gamma n_\alpha^{-1}=U_{s_\alpha\gamma}$ as subgroup schemes.

Let $K\subseteq G$ be reductive and contain $T$. The torus remains fibrewise maximal in $K$. By [lem-ag-smooth-relative-differentials-finite-locally-free] and [lem-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials-base-change], dual-number tangents of $K$ are finite projective and commute with base change. Apply [lem-sfb-relative-torus-bundle-weights] to their full coaction. The closed immersion gives injective tangent maps on every geometric fibre. Thus each nonzero weight is a root of $G$, and each weight summand has fibre rank zero or one. Refine the base by the finitely many clopen rank patterns. On each piece the rank-one summands map isomorphically to the corresponding free root lines of $G$: a map of line bundles nonzero on every residue field is multiplication locally by a unit. Hence $K$ has the framing needed for steps 1--2 on that piece. For a root $\gamma$ of $K$ the composite of its exponential with $K\hookrightarrow G$ has the differential and equivariance of $\exp_\gamma$, so uniqueness identifies both. This also constructs its root exponential independently of the rank-pattern cover.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.4 uniqueness; Section 4.2 rank-one centralizers, and compatibility under reductive overgroups.

proof.text: In particular, when $K$ has root $\gamma$, apply [lem-sfb-relative-root-rank-one-centralizer] to $(K,T)$ and the rank-one line $\operatorname{Lie}(K)_\gamma=\mathfrak g_\gamma$ of step 6: its $-\gamma$ weight module is locally free of rank one, so $-\gamma$ is a root of $K$ and $\operatorname{Lie}(K)_{-\gamma}=\mathfrak g_{-\gamma}$ by step 6. The rank-one centralizer $Z_K(T_\gamma)$ then goes through [lem-sfb-reductive-framed-noetherian-descent], [lem-sfb-relative-rank-one-local-matrix-model] and [lem-sfb-relative-split-torus-matrix-sheaf] exactly as in steps 4--5. Its two root modules and exponentials are those of $G$. Applying the rank-one calculation of steps 4--5 inside $K$ produces a generator whose three-exponential word normalizes $T$ also in $G$. Uniqueness in step 4, valid for any root with a chosen generator, makes its linked generator and its word equal to those in $G$. The two reflection formulas then give equality of the coroots after precomposition by $\gamma:T\to\mathbf G_m$. This character is an fppf epimorphism: write $\gamma=d\gamma_0$ with $\gamma_0$ primitive, choose a lattice basis beginning with $\gamma_0$, and lift a unit $c$ after the finite free faithfully flat algebra $R[z]/(z^d-c)$, where $z$ is a unit. Equality after this cover implies equality of the coroot homomorphisms by [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent]. This proves both subgroup-compatibility assertions, without assuming the root data of $K$ and $G$ agree outside the specified root.

source.place: Section 4.2 construction of coroots and Corollary 5.1.9 proof: reduction through a common rank-one subgroup.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-relative-torus-automorphism-fixed-group] to conjugation by $T$ on $G$. It gives a smooth affine finitely presented centralizer $C=Z_G(T)$ with connected geometric fibres, commuting with base change. On each geometric fibre $T\hookrightarrow C$ is an isomorphism by [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-self-centralizer]. Thus [lem-sfb-flat-geometric-fibre-open-criterion] applied to this closed inclusion between smooth schemes gives $C=T$ over $A$. This is scheme-theoretic and holds on nonreduced test algebras.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.9(2), pp.85--86, together with connectedness of reductive torus centralizers.

proof.text: Let $W$ be the subgroup of lattice automorphisms generated by all root reflections. It is finite by [lem-sfb-finite-root-datum-weyl-group]. It is already generated by the simple reflections: apply [lem-sfb-root-base-reflection-induction] to the property $s_\gamma\in\langle s_\alpha:\alpha\in\Delta\rangle$. It holds for simple roots, is unchanged by negation, and is preserved by a simple reflection because $s_{s_\alpha\gamma}=s_\alpha s_\gamma s_\alpha^{-1}$. The rational root pairing and its base here are supplied by [lem-sfb-root-datum-lattice-embedding] and [lem-sfb-root-base-rational-integral-spans]; apply them on the root span, so central lattice directions cause no spanning assumption on $M$. Choose a word in the $n_\alpha$ for each $w\in W$, giving $n_w\in N_G(T)(A)$.

source.place: Proposition 5.1.6, p.138, and Corollary 5.1.11 proof, pp.142--143.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-relative-torus-centralizer-normalizer], the normalizer is smooth and decomposes into open and closed action loci $N_\sigma$, indexed by lattice automorphisms. Its geometric fibres act through $W$: each geometric fibre has the Borel subgroup $P(\lambda)\supseteq T$ for a regular cocharacter $\lambda$ by [lem-sfb-regular-cocharacter-borel-description], so [lem-sfb-weyl-reflection-realization] applies and identifies their quotient by the torus with the reflection group; the representatives just constructed give all those reflections on the full character lattice. Thus $N_\sigma$ is empty unless $\sigma$ is an action arising from $W$. For each $w$, multiplication by $n_w$ identifies its action locus with the kernel action locus, which is $Z_G(T)=T$ by step 8. Consequently $N_G(T)=\coprod_{w\in W}n_wT$ and its quotient sheaf is $\underline W$. On a disconnected base its sections are locally constant $W$-valued functions. The element $(n_\alpha n_\beta)^{m_{\alpha\beta}}$ maps to $(s_\alpha s_\beta)^{m_{\alpha\beta}}=1$, so it lies in the kernel $T(A)$.

source.place: Proposition 5.1.6 and Corollary 5.1.11; the action convention for characters can invert the index but gives the same action loci and cosets.

proof.text: Choose an integral cocharacter $\lambda$ positive on $\Delta$, by giving the linearly independent simple roots value $1$ in the rational dual, extending to $M\otimes\mathbf Q$, and clearing denominators. It is nonzero on every root. By [lem-sfb-relative-dynamic-subgroups], $U^\pm=U_G(\pm\lambda)$ are smooth closed subgroups, and $U^-\times Z_G(\lambda)\times U^+\to G$ is an open immersion. On geometric fibres $Z_G(\lambda)=T$: its connected smooth fibre has Lie algebra $\mathfrak t$. The inclusion of $T$ has isomorphic tangents at every point by translation, hence is etale by [lem-sfb-smooth-tangent-isomorphism-etale] and open by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-closed-immersion-open]. Being also closed and nonempty, its image is the whole connected fibre. Apply [lem-sfb-flat-geometric-fibre-open-criterion] to conclude $Z_G(\lambda)=T$ over $A$. Each positive root map lands in $U^+$ by contraction. Over a geometric fibre, [lem-sfb-regular-cocharacter-borel-description] makes $P_G(\lambda)$ a Borel. Its unipotent radical $R_u$ has the ordered root coordinates of [lem-sfb-borel-root-product-coordinates]. Every positive root group lies in the subgroup $U^+$ by contraction, so $R_u$, the image of their ordered product, is a closed subgroup of $U^+$. Both are smooth and connected with tangent space $\bigoplus_{\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle>0}\mathfrak g_\alpha$ (by [lem-sfb-relative-dynamic-subgroups] and the coordinates of [lem-sfb-borel-root-product-coordinates]); the etale closed-inclusion argument just given identifies them. Thus the multiplication of its positive root groups in any order is a fibrewise isomorphism. The same fibre criterion makes each ordered product an isomorphism to $U^+$ over $A$. Apply this to $-\lambda$ as well. It identifies the open immersion with the asserted $\Omega$, and proves positive-system coordinates for every regular cocharacter, not just the initial $\Delta$.

For the closed set $\Psi$, its stated closure under all nonempty root sums implies the binary closure in [lem-sfb-closed-root-set-positive-functional]. Choose its regular $\lambda$ positive on $\Psi$ and use step 11 for the ambient positive system $\Sigma=\Phi_{\lambda>0}$. For any ordering of a subset $E\subseteq\Sigma$, its product is a smooth closed subscheme of $U_\Sigma$: extend the enumeration to all of $\Sigma$ and set the other affine root coordinates equal to zero in the ordered-product isomorphism. Apply [lem-sfb-equivariant-root-commutator-support] to these root coordinates. For $a,b\in\Psi$ its commutator roots $ia+jb$ remain in $\Psi$, by the strong closure stipulated in the item. Thus the commutator of two root factors only introduces factors at strictly larger $\lambda$-height. No assumption that the structure constants are units is used.

Prove by descending induction on $m\geq1$ that the height-ordered coordinate subscheme for $\Psi_{\geq m}=\{c\in\Psi:\lambda(c)\geq m\}$ is a subgroup $V_m$. For $m$ above all root heights it is the identity. Suppose $V_{m+1}$ is a subgroup. The commutator formula in step 12 shows that each root group at height $m$ normalizes $V_{m+1}$: commute it past the latter's root factors; all additional roots have height at least $m+1$ and belong to $\Psi$. Two factors at height $m$ commute modulo $V_{m+1}$, since every commutator root has height at least $2m\geq m+1$. Their images in the quotient of their common pointwise normalizer by $V_{m+1}$ therefore form commuting subgroups. Their product, lifted and multiplied by $V_{m+1}$, is a subgroup on every algebra's points, including under inverses. Its coordinate subscheme is exactly the height-ordered product for $\Psi_{\geq m}$. Yoneda gives a subgroup scheme $V_m$, which is smooth and closed by step 12. For any other enumeration, its multiplication factors through $V_1$ and is invertible by finite height recursion: modulo $V_2$ the height-one parameters are the coordinates in the product of the height-one additive root groups. Choose these parameters to match a prescribed element of $V_1$. Having matched modulo $V_m$, the discrepancy in $V_m/V_{m+1}$ has unique additive coordinates indexed by height-$m$ roots, since the height-ordered chart is unique and the commutators have larger height. Set the still undetermined height-$m$ parameters to cancel this discrepancy. Changing them cannot alter lower-height coordinates, regardless of their positions in the chosen enumeration. The recursion terminates above the largest root height and constructs mutually inverse maps on every algebra's points. All operations are multiplication, inverse and extraction of the height-ordered polynomial coordinates, so the inverses are natural in the algebra. Yoneda proves that every enumeration is an isomorphism onto $V_1$. This is $U_\Psi$.

source.place: Proposition 5.1.16 proof, pp.147--148; explicit descending-height subgroup induction and comparison of enumerations.

proof.text: For distinct simple roots $\alpha,\beta$, the set $\Psi_{\alpha\beta}$ is closed in the stated strong sense: addition adds its nonnegative simple-root coefficients. It has no opposite pair because the base is linearly independent. If $c=i\alpha+j\beta\ne\alpha$ is in it, then $j>0$; reducedness excludes $i\alpha$ except $\alpha$. The root $s_\alpha c$ still has coefficient $j>0$ on $\beta$ and zero coefficients outside $\alpha,\beta$. Every root's simple coefficients have one sign, so its coefficient on $\alpha$ is also nonnegative. Hence $s_\alpha c\in\Psi_{\alpha\beta}$. Step 5 now gives $n_\alpha U_c n_\alpha^{-1}=U_{s_\alpha c}\subseteq U_{\Psi_{\alpha\beta}}$. Interchange $\alpha$ and $\beta$ for the second assertion.

source.place: Root-datum base axioms; application of Corollary 5.1.9 and Proposition 5.1.16 in Section 6.2.

proof.text: The group multiplication $G\times_AG\to G$ becomes the projection to the second factor after the isomorphism $(x,y)\mapsto(x,xy)$, with inverse $(x,z)\mapsto(x,x^{-1}z)$. It is smooth: its affine-ring projection is base change of the smooth structure map of $G$, by [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-ring-map-iff-smooth-affine] and [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-ring-map-base-change-composition]. The inclusion $\Omega\times\Omega\subseteq G\times G$ is open, using [lem-weil-pbc-open-immersion-base-change], so its multiplication is smooth by [lem-pc-open-immersion-smooth-composition], hence flat and locally of finite presentation by [lem-pc-smooth-flat]. It is surjective on geometric fibres. Indeed each fibre $G_F$ is irreducible by [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component], and for $g\in G_F(F)$ the nonempty opens $\Omega_F$ and $g\Omega_F^{-1}$ intersect. Choose a geometric point of their intersection, allowing a field extension $F'/F$; it writes $g=xy$ with $x,y\in\Omega_F(F')$. The same argument applies over an algebraic closure of the residue field of any point of $G$, proving surjectivity on the whole underlying space. Thus this map is faithfully flat and locally of finite presentation. Its pullback along any test point supplies an fppf covering on which that point is a product of two open-cell elements; their root-and-torus coordinates prove sheaf generation.

source.place: Section 6.2 opening paragraph, printed p.198; smoothness and geometric-fibre argument for multiplication of two open cells.

proof.text: Finally the framed model of step 1 has semisimple rank $\dim_{\mathbf Q}\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf Q}\Phi$ on every geometric fibre by the explicit rank assertion of [lem-sfb-reductive-framed-noetherian-descent]. Every geometric fibre of $G$ is a field extension of such a fibre of this model, so this is the required rank for $G$. No preceding construction required a connected or reduced base. If $\Phi=\varnothing$, the centralizer computation of step 8 gives $G=T$, all root products are the identity, $\Omega=T$, and the Weyl quotient and root span have rank zero. If $\Psi=\varnothing$, the descending induction starts and ends at the identity subgroup. These cases therefore satisfy all clauses as well.

source.place: Section 1.3 root rank, and empty-root case of Theorem 5.1.13 and Proposition 5.1.16.
